title: Fortitude (ST II-II.123)
hook: courage is mostly endurance, not attack

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice: a steady will to give each person, and God, their due. Your line was each their due. What small debt did you pay that nobody was chasing? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

Two kinds of brave. The first runs into the burning building. It's sudden, loud, and it makes the evening news. The second sits in a plastic chair beside a hospital bed through a long night, and then the next night, and then the next. Nobody films it. There's nothing to charge at. There's only staying. Ask the evening news which one is courage, and the first one wins. Ask Thomas Aquinas, and you get a different answer. He's walking through the cardinal virtues: prudence, then justice. Today the third. Fortitude.
screen: `THE BURNING BUILDING.` → `THE PLASTIC CHAIR, NIGHT AFTER NIGHT.` → `WHICH ONE IS COURAGE?`

segments.voice: Fortitude, for Thomas, is the virtue that keeps a person steady in the good when fear pushes them to quit. It deals with two things: fear, which makes us want to run, and daring, which can make us reckless. Fortitude holds the line between them. And then his surprising claim. The main act of fortitude, he says, isn't attacking. It's enduring: standing firm. He gives reasons. When you attack, you're usually the stronger one in that moment. When you endure, something stronger is pressing on you. Attack looks to a danger that's still ahead; endurance faces one that's already here. And attack can be over in a flash, while endurance has to last. So for Thomas, staying is often harder than charging. The plastic chair, not the burning building. Thomas has in mind above all the gravest dangers, standing firm even before death, and he calls martyrdom the highest act of this virtue. The Catechism describes fortitude more broadly, as firmness in difficulties and constancy in pursuing the good. That widens it to ordinary life: the long illness, the job you can't leave yet, the child who isn't sleeping, the grief that won't hurry. Jesus says to his disciples, in the Douay-Rheims: "but he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved." Persevere. Not win, not storm the gates. Last. Fortitude isn't the absence of fear, either. Thomas assumes the fear is there. That's what the virtue is for. A person with fortitude feels the full weight, and doesn't put down the good thing they're carrying.
screen: `STEADY WHEN FEAR SAYS QUIT.` · `THE MAIN ACT IS ENDURING.` · `STAYING IS HARDER THAN CHARGING.` · `NOT FEARLESS: FAITHFUL.` · then, large: `HE THAT SHALL PERSEVERE UNTO THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: endure one hard thing calmly. Settle, and breathe. Name one hard thing you're carrying that won't be fixed today. A worry. A difficult person. A body that hurts. A season that's lasting too long. Don't try to solve it now. Just let it be there, and breathe beside it, the way someone sits beside a hospital bed. Notice the urge to run from it, into distraction or into anger. Let the urge come, and stay anyway. Slow your breath. Loosen your shoulders. You're not attacking it. You're standing firm next to it. If you pray, you can ask God for strength for today only. The bell holds the time.
Fortitude. For Thomas, the steadiness to hold to the good in the face of fear, whose main act is enduring, not attacking. Today's word.
Your line: endure. Today, when the hard thing shows up again, stay with it one minute longer than you want to, calmly, without a fight. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching counts fortitude among the four cardinal virtues and among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and Catholics honor the martyrs as its highest witnesses while also praying for strength in illness, grief and ordinary trials.

myth: for Thomas, the main act of courage is attacking
he says the main act of fortitude is enduring: standing firm when something stronger presses.
Thomas thinks enduring is harder than attacking
the one who endures faces something stronger, already present, for a long time.
Thomas assumes the fear is there. the virtue keeps a person steady in the good despite it.

fork.setup: you're facing something hard that won't be fixed today: a long illness in the family. what does Thomas call the main act of fortitude here?
options: charge at it and force it to end.
endure: stand firm and stay steady in the good.
get away from it as fast as possible.
fork.reveal: Thomas says fortitude's chief act is endurance, not attack, because staying under pressure is harder than charging.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: strength, firmness of mind in the face of danger.

trapdoor: what you thought: courage means charging in.
what it means: for Thomas, courage is mostly endurance, staying steady in the good when fear says quit.
what a scholar hears: Thomas says enduring is harder than attacking: a stronger foe, a present danger, and a long time, so endurance is the chief act.
recall: a firm habit of doing good

sources.quoted: but he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: fortitude concerns fear and daring (II-II.123.3); chiefly about dangers of death (II-II.123.4); the principal act is endurance rather than attack, with three reasons (a stronger opponent, present rather than future danger, long duration) (II-II.123.6 ad 1); martyrdom as the most perfect act of fortitude (II-II.124.3).
The Catechism's broader description (firmness in difficulties, constancy in pursuing the good) is paraphrased from CCC 1808.
howItsDone says fortitude is among the gifts of the Holy Spirit (Isaiah 11:2 in the Vulgate tradition; CCC 1831); confirm.
